title: A Kitchen for the Postcard
premise: Felix Lockridge, a pastry chef whose Copenhagen-style café is three missed payments from collapse, has spent ten years writing anonymous letters to a stranger he once saved from a breakdown on a train platform—letters that became the other person's lifeline. When Marlow Voss, the letter recipient, moves in next door and begins piecing together who 'the postcard writer' really is, Felix's carefully contained heart and carefully hidden identity both start to crack. As the café faces foreclosure and a lucrative TV competition offers salvation at the cost of exposing his private self, Felix must decide whether loyalty to the person he invented is worth more than the truth of who he actually is. In the end, Felix loses the café but wins the competition's consolation prize—a book deal built on the letters—and chooses to sign his real name, finally visible, to both the pages and to Marlow.
about_author: Petra Eriksen is a former line cook who spent six years writing letters she never sent before turning the habit into fiction. She lives above a bakery in a coastal town, where she claims the smell of proofing dough is the only alarm clock she trusts.

chapters.title: Three Payments
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Opening on a gray Tuesday audit: the café is three missed payments from gone, and Felix rehearses his philosophy that the heart is a trainable muscle. He writes letter #117 that night, anonymous as always. Emotional beat: controlled dread masked as discipline.

chapters.title: The Moving Truck
chapters.summary: Marlow's POV. A new neighbor arrives with boxes labeled by decade and a wall of saved letters. Marlow recognizes the handwriting instantly but says nothing when they meet Felix over borrowed sugar. Emotional beat: quiet, electric recognition held behind courtesy.

chapters.title: Cardamom and Confession
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Felix caters a small welcome gathering; Marlow quotes a line from letter #40 back to him as if it were their own thought. Felix nearly drops a tray. Neither names what's happening. Emotional beat: the thrill and terror of being half-seen.

chapters.title: What the Letters Were For
chapters.summary: Marlow's POV. Flashback to the train platform crisis ten years ago and how the first anonymous letter arrived a week later. Marlow explains to their sister why they kept writing back to someone who never signed. Emotional beat: tenderness braided with unresolved debt.

chapters.title: Foreclosure Notice
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The bank letter arrives taped to the café door. Felix's business partner Rune urges selling the recipes; Felix refuses—the recipes are the letters' twin, too personal to monetize. Emotional beat: pride curdling into panic.

chapters.title: The Competition
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A televised baking competition offers a prize that could save everything—but contestants must share personal stories on camera. Felix applies anyway, planning to fabricate a palatable past. Emotional beat: desperate hope wearing a mask.

chapters.title: Sunday Mornings
chapters.summary: Both POVs interleaved. An accidental ritual forms: Marlow brings coffee, Felix brings failed test bakes, and they talk about everything except the letters. Emotional beat: intimacy growing in the space between two deliberate silences.

chapters.title: Letter #121
chapters.summary: Marlow's POV. Marlow writes back to the anonymous stranger for the first time in years—telling the stranger about falling for the neighbor—and mails it to the old drop box. Emotional beat: guilt sharpening into clarity about divided loyalties.

chapters.title: Rune's Offer
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Rune secretly pitches the letters' story to the show's producers without Felix's consent. The producers love it: 'the anonymous pen pal angle.' Felix feels betrayed twice over—by Rune, and by how tempting exposure suddenly is. Emotional beat: violation and appetite in the same breath.

chapters.title: Almost
chapters.summary: Both POVs. A near-kiss interrupted by a producer's call. Afterward, Marlow almost confesses knowing about the letters; Felix almost confesses writing them. Both retreat. Emotional beat: the ache of parallel cowardice.

chapters.title: The Drop Box
chapters.summary: Marlow's POV. Marlow stakes out the old drop box and watches Felix collect mail—including Marlow's own letter #121 reply. The truth lands physically: the neighbor and the stranger are one person. Emotional beat: heartbreak and revelation fused.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Competition rehearsal forces Felix to script his 'authentic' story. He writes a version of himself that is charming and false, and hates how easily it comes. Emotional beat: self-alienation dressed as professionalism.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Marlow's POV. Marlow confronts Felix mid-bake, letter #121 on the counter between them. Felix denies nothing but offers no apology either: 'You loved the letters. I'm the liability.' Marlow leaves. Emotional beat: truth delivered like a blade wrapped in a towel.

chapters.title: Silence, Proofed
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Days of silence. Felix throws himself into competition prep while the café's final notice posts publicly. Rune quits. Felix realizes the muscle-training metaphor was always just fear with better posture. Emotional beat: rock bottom, quietly lit.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Both POVs. On air, asked why he started writing letters, Felix abandons the script and tells the truth—the platform, the decade, the neighbor next door. Marlow watches from the café's darkened window across town. Emotional beat: public vulnerability as private apology.

chapters.title: Second Place
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix doesn't win the prize money but wins the audience—and a publisher's offer to publish the letters, unredacted, under his real name. The bank takes the café lease regardless. Emotional beat: loss and arrival occupying the same hour.

chapters.title: Empty Cases
chapters.summary: Marlow's POV. Marlow helps pack the café, and among the boxes finds every draft, every unsent reply Felix never mailed. Understanding replaces anger: Felix wasn't hiding from Marlow; he was hiding from being known. Emotional beat: compassion after betrayal.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix writes letter #122—signed, hand-delivered, slipped under Marlow's door at dawn: an apology, an accounting, and a question. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into courage.

chapters.title: Reply
chapters.summary: Marlow's POV. Marlow reads it twice, then walks to the shuttered café where Felix sits amid empty shelves. No speeches—just Marlow sliding a fresh sheet of paper across the counter: 'Start over. Out loud this time.' Emotional beat: forgiveness as invitation.

chapters.title: New Lease
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The publisher advances enough for a tiny new space—not a café but a letter-writing room with a coffee cart, co-run. They argue happily about the name. Emotional beat: rebuilding as courtship.

chapters.title: A Kitchen for the Postcard
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Launch day of the book and the little shop. Felix reads the first page aloud to a room of strangers, voice steady, Marlow's hand in his. The heart, it turns out, was never containable—only waiting. Emotional beat: belonging earned, not granted.

chapters.title: Epilogue: Postmark
chapters.summary: Marlow's POV, one year later. A customer mails a letter from the shop's corner desk; Felix bakes; Marlow pins letter #1 beside letter #122 on the wall. Final image: two names on the door, neither anonymous. Emotional beat: memory honored, truth chosen, home made.
